beats.lead: London did not fix its sewage problem out of foresight.
beats.text: It fixed it because, in the summer of 1858, the smell became unbearable, even to the people who ran the country.
beats.note: By the 1850s London held a couple of million people, and roughly half a billion litres of Thames water were drawn back into homes and businesses every day, the very river that carried away the city's sewage.

beats.text: On 16 June 1858 the temperature in London reached 35 degrees Celsius, the peak of a summer that stayed above 30 degrees for weeks.
beats.note: Blinds in the new Palace of Westminster were soaked in chloride of lime so members could bear to sit inside. The engineer responsible for ventilating the building told the Speaker he could no longer be answerable for the health of the House.

beats.lead: The smell was blamed for the wrong thing, and acting on it still worked.
beats.text: Doctors and MPs believed foul air itself, not water, spread the cholera and typhoid going around that summer.
beats.note: That theory, called miasma, was wrong. But the same stench that frightened Parliament also happened to sit directly over the source of the real, waterborne disease, so a false fear still led to a genuine fix.

beats.name: Joseph Bazalgette
beats.role: Chief engineer of the Metropolitan Board of Works. Chancellor Benjamin Disraeli introduced his sewer funding bill on 15 July 1858, and it became law just eighteen days later, on 2 August.

beats.context: Length of the new intercepting sewers Bazalgette's team built alongside the Thames, on top of over a thousand miles of smaller street sewers, work that ran from 1859 to 1875.

beats.text: By 1887, the sewage that had once floated past Parliament had stopped going into the Thames at all.

beats.line: The smell did what years of warnings could not: it got London's sewers built.
